chapter_summary:
Secure Shell (SSH) is the backbone of remote administration for RHEL systems, providing a secure, encrypted channel for command-line access, file transfers, and tunnel creation. While basic password authentication is convenient, it's inherently vulnerable to brute-force attacks. The first and most critical step in advanced SSH security is to transition to **key-based authentication**. This method uses a pair of cryptographic keys: a private key, kept secret on your local machine, and a public key, stored on the remote server. When you attempt to connect, the server challenges your client, which responds using its private key. If the keys match, access is granted without ever sending a password over the network. This is significantly more secure as private keys are much harder to guess or crack than passwords, especially when protected with a strong passphrase.

To generate an SSH key pair, you use the `ssh-keygen` command on your local machine:
```bash
ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4000 -C "your_email@example.com"
```
This command creates an RSA key pair with a 4000-bit length (a good practice for security) and includes a comment for identification. You'll be prompted to save the key to a file (default `~/.ssh/id_rsa`) and to enter a passphrase. **Always use a strong passphrase for your private key.** This encrypts your private key on disk, providing an extra layer of security if your local machine is compromised. Once generated, your public key will be in `~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub`. To install the public key on a remote server, the `ssh-copy-id` utility is the most convenient method:
```bash
ssh-copy-id username@remote_host
```
This command securely copies your public key to the `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` file on the remote server, setting the correct permissions automatically. If `ssh-copy-id` isn't available or you prefer manual transfer, you can use `scp` to copy the public key and then append it to `authorized_keys` while ensuring correct permissions (`chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys` and `chmod 700 ~/.ssh`).

Once key-based authentication is set up, you should harden the SSH daemon (`sshd`) configuration on the server. The main configuration file is `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`. **The most important security hardening step is to disable password authentication entirely.** This forces all connections to use key-based authentication.
```ini
# In /etc/ssh/sshd_config
PasswordAuthentication no
```
Another critical directive is `PermitRootLogin`. **It is highly recommended to set `PermitRootLogin no`** to prevent direct root logins, even with keys. Instead, log in as a regular user and then use `sudo` for administrative tasks. This adds an extra barrier against attackers targeting the root account. You can further restrict access by allowing only specific users or groups using `AllowUsers` or `AllowGroups` directives. For example:
```ini
# In /etc/ssh/sshd_config
AllowUsers alice bob
```
This ensures only `alice` and `bob` can SSH into the server. After making any changes to `sshd_config`, you must restart the SSH service: `sudo systemctl restart sshd`. A common mistake is forgetting to restart the service, leading to confusion when changes don't take effect. Always test your changes thoroughly from another session before logging out of your current administrative session, especially when disabling password authentication or root login, to avoid locking yourself out.

For client-side convenience and security, the `~/.ssh/config` file allows you to define aliases and specific settings for different hosts. This can include specifying a different username, a custom private key file, or port forwarding rules.
```ini
# In ~/.ssh/config on your local machine
Host myserver
    Hostname 192.168.1.100
    User adminuser
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_rsa_myserver
    Port 2222 # If SSH runs on a non-standard port
```
Now, you can simply type `ssh myserver` to connect. For managing multiple SSH keys without repeatedly typing passphrases, the `ssh-agent` is invaluable. It holds your decrypted private keys in memory for the duration of your session. You can start the agent (`eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"`) and add your keys (`ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_rsa`). This allows you to use your keys without entering the passphrase for each connection.

Security notes: Always keep your private key secure and never share it. If your private key is compromised, immediately revoke access by removing its corresponding public key from `authorized_keys` on all affected servers. Regularly review `sshd_config` for any unintended open permissions or outdated settings. Keep your SSH client and server software updated to patch known vulnerabilities. By implementing key-based authentication, hardening `sshd_config`, and managing client configurations, you establish a robust and secure remote access strategy for your RHEL systems.

screens.title: Advanced SSH Configuration and Security
screens.subtitle: Strengthen remote access with keys, hardened server settings, and managed client workflows

narration.text: SSH is the primary secure channel you use to manage RHEL systems remotely. In this lesson you will learn why key-based authentication replaces passwords, how to generate and install keys safely, and how to harden the SSH daemon so attackers cannot brute-force or directly access the root account. You will also see practical client-side workflows: using an SSH agent to avoid repeated passphrases, and a local SSH config to simplify connections. The goal is a workflow where your private key stays protected on your machine, the server accepts only verified public keys, and server configuration forces stronger authentication and limits who can connect. A concrete example we'll use throughout is creating a 4096-bit RSA key pair, copying the public key to an administrative user, and then disabling password logins and root access on the server. A common pitfall is locking yourself out by changing server settings without a fallback session; we'll show safe testing patterns so you can apply changes and verify them. By the end you'll understand both commands and the reasoning behind each hardening step.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Key-based SSH plus careful sshd configuration reduces attack surface and makes remote administration both secure and convenient.

Why this matters

Key Takeaway

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will implement key-based SSH authentication and configure the server to reject passwords and direct root logins. You will also build client-side workflows with ssh-agent and a local SSH config file so connections are both secure and efficient. Each objective focuses on a practical skill: generate and protect key pairs, copy the public key to the server and confirm permissions, edit and test sshd configuration directives safely, and manage agent-held keys for multiple sessions. For example, you'll generate a 4096-bit RSA key pair, copy the public key to an administrative user on a RHEL server, then set PasswordAuthentication to no and PermitRootLogin to no while testing from an open session to avoid lockout. You will learn to restart the sshd service after changes and to use AllowUsers or AllowGroups to narrow access. Finally, you'll know how to revoke keys, remove entries from authorized_keys, and rotate keys if a private key is compromised. These objectives focus on safety, verification, and recoverability so your hardening steps are effective and reversible.

narration.text: Beyond configuration commands, you'll practice safe change procedures that prevent accidental lockout. You'll also be able to restrict access using AllowUsers or AllowGroups so only named administrators can connect. Verification & Recovery

Change management and testing procedures that protect your access while hardening SSH.

Test first

Permissions
Correct file modes

Common misconception

screens.title: Why key-based authentication is stronger than passwords
screens.subtitle: Public/private key pairs reduce attack surface and avoid password exposure

narration.text: Key-based authentication uses an asymmetric key pair: a private key that stays on your local machine and a public key that the server stores to verify you. The private key is never sent across the network; instead the server sends a challenge that only the holder of the private key can answer. Practically, this prevents remote attackers from guessing a password because they would need the private key file itself. A strong passphrase on the private key protects it from physical theft of the file. For example, generating a 4096-bit RSA key creates a pair where the private key is unreadable without its passphrase and the public key is safe to distribute to servers. Common misconceptions include thinking key files are insecure if not encrypted — always use a passphrase — and that key-based auth removes the need for account-level controls; it does not. You should still restrict which users can login on the server and monitor authorized_keys. When keys are used with ssh-agent, you get convenience without storing the passphrase on disk. The main takeaway is that key-based authentication raises the bar against brute-force and credential-reuse attacks while remaining practical for administrators who follow passphrase and agent best practices.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Keys authenticate by possession of a private key plus optional passphrase; public keys verify identity on the server.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Key-based Authentication
What it is

An asymmetric pair: the private key stays local and is used to prove identity; the public key is appended to the server's authorized_keys to allow access.

Analogy
Think of the private key as a physical key in your pocket and the public key as a lock on the server. Possessing the key lets you open the lock without sending a copy of the key across the street.
Benefit
Resists brute-force
Note
Protect private key with passphrase
Concrete example
ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "admin@example.com"
# follow prompts, use a strong passphrase
# public key saved to ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub
Misconception
Some think a public key can be secret. Public keys are safe to copy to servers. The private key must never be shared; if leaked, rotate keys immediately.
Key Takeaway

Key pairs protect credentials by possession and are stronger than passwords when private keys are passphrase-protected and managed correctly.

screens.title: Generate and install SSH keys
screens.subtitle: Commands and safe steps for creating keys and copying the public key to a RHEL server

narration.text: Generating and installing keys is an operational task you will perform every time you provision secure access. Start on your local machine with ssh-keygen. Choose a modern algorithm and a long key length; for example, RSA 4096 is commonly used for compatibility and strength. When prompted, accept the default file path unless you need multiple keys for different hosts, in which case name them clearly. Always use a strong passphrase. After generation, install the public key on the server with ssh-copy-id which appends and fixes permissions for you. If ssh-copy-id is not available, copy the public key with scp and then append it to ~/. ssh/authorized_keys on the server, ensuring ~/. ssh has 700 and authorized_keys 600. A live example: run ssh-keygen, then ssh-copy-id adminuser@<REMOTE_SERVER_IP>. If the server has a nonstandard port, include the -p flag when copying. Always test the new login from another terminal so you confirm the key works before making server-side hardening changes. A common failure is incorrect permissions on ~/. ssh or authorized_keys; if the key is rejected, check file modes first. Practice this sequence until it is repeatable and safe.

keyIdea.title: Command pattern
keyIdea.text: ssh-keygen → ssh-copy-id (or scp + append) → verify permissions → test login from a separate session.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Generate & Install Keys
Step-by-step
1. Generate a key pair
ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "my_admin_key@myclient"
2. Copy public key to server
ssh-copy-id adminuser@<REMOTE_SERVER_IP>
# or scp ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub adminuser@<REMOTE_SERVER_IP>:~/
# then on server: mkdir -p ~/.ssh; cat id_rsa.pub >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
3. Fix permissions
chmod 700 ~/.ssh
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
Common failure modes
  • Authorized keys rejected because ~/.ssh is world-writable or authorized_keys has wrong mode.
  • Used a weak or empty passphrase; private key should be protected.
  • Copied a private key by mistake instead of the public key.
Example scenario
You generate a key on workstation A, use ssh-copy-id to install it on adminuser@192.0.2.10, then open a new terminal and run ssh adminuser@192.0.2.10 to verify access without a password.
Key Takeaway

Use ssh-copy-id when available; otherwise copy the public key and set strict permissions before testing a key-based login.

screens.title: Permissions and authorized_keys details
screens.subtitle: Why file modes matter and how to avoid the most common rejections

narration.text: SSH enforces strict file permissions for security. The directory ~/. ssh must normally be mode 700 (only the owner can read, write, or execute), and ~/. ssh/authorized_keys should be 600 (owner read/write only). If these files are more permissive, the SSH daemon will refuse key-based authentication because it treats those files as a potential vector for tampering. A typical failure is using scp to copy authorized_keys but leaving the file world-readable; the server then rejects the key and falls back to password authentication or denies login entirely. Always set permissions immediately after creating or editing authorized_keys. Another detail: the home directory itself should not allow group or other write access, because some configurations check parent directory permissions. When you transfer a key manually, verify ownership and modes with ls -ld and chmod/chown as needed. For example, run chmod 700 ~/. ssh and chmod 600 ~/. ssh/authorized_keys on the server. If keys still fail, review /var/log/secure or journalctl -u sshd for specific rejection reasons. This diagnostic step saves time and avoids unnecessary reconfiguration changes. Permissions and authorized_keys details means strict file and directory modes are required for ssh to accept public keys; check and fix modes before changing sshd settings.. In practical terms, why file modes matter and how to avoid the most common rejections. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Permissions rule
keyIdea.text: Strict file and directory modes are required for SSH to accept public keys; check and fix modes before changing sshd settings.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Permissions & authorized_keys
Required modes
chmod 700 ~/.ssh
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
# ensure home is not writable by group/others
If keys fail, check ownership and file modes. SSH often logs authentication rejections with messages pointing to insecure permissions; consult the system log to confirm the cause.
Diagnostic checklist
  • Is ~/.ssh owned by the user? (ls -ld ~/.ssh)
  • Are permissions 700 for ~/.ssh and 600 for authorized_keys?
  • Is the user's home directory not writable by group/others?
  • Are there duplicate keys or malformed lines in authorized_keys?
Example log
sshd[1234]: Authentication refused: bad ownership or modes for directory /home/adminuser
Key Takeaway

Correct ownership and strict modes are prerequisites for key authentication; fix permissions before assuming configuration errors.

screens.title: Hardening sshd_config
screens.subtitle: Key directives: PasswordAuthentication, PermitRootLogin, AllowUsers / AllowGroups

narration.text: The SSH daemon is controlled by /etc/ssh/sshd_config. To harden the server, three directives are most important. First, set PasswordAuthentication no to force key-based login only. That prevents brute-force password attempts. Second, set PermitRootLogin no to stop direct root logins. Instead, administrators should log in as a regular user and use sudo. This reduces the target surface for attackers who often try root directly. Third, use AllowUsers or AllowGroups to list permitted accounts, which narrows access to known administrators. For example, adding AllowUsers adminuser alice will restrict logins to those names. After editing sshd_config you must restart the sshd service with sudo systemctl restart sshd; failing to restart is a common cause of seeing no effect. Always test changes from another session before you close your current administrative connection. A misconception is thinking these settings alone secure the server; they are necessary but not sufficient — you still must manage keys, keep software updated, and monitor logs. Together, these directives form the backbone of server-side access control for SSH. Hardening sshd_config means disable password logins, disallow root, and restrict which users or groups may connect to reduce exposure.. In practical terms, key directives: passwordauthentication, permitrootlogin, allowusers / allowgroups. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Hardening trio
keyIdea.text: Disable password logins, disallow root, and restrict which users or groups may connect to reduce exposure.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › sshd Hardening
Directive
PasswordAuthentication no
Forces key-based authentication only; prevents brute-force password attempts.
PermitRootLogin no
Prevents direct root SSH. Use a regular user + sudo for administrative tasks.
AllowUsers / AllowGroups
Limit logins to specific users or groups for tighter access control and auditability.
Example edits
# In /etc/ssh/sshd_config
PasswordAuthentication no
PermitRootLogin no
AllowUsers adminuser alice
Restart required: sudo systemctl restart sshd. Test login from another terminal before closing your current session to avoid accidental lockout.
Common mistake

Editing sshd_config without a live test and restart often results in confusion; remember to restart and verify from a separate session.

screens.title: Restarting sshd and safe verification
screens.subtitle: Verify changes without losing access — a safe operational checklist

narration.text: Restarting sshd is required for configuration changes to take effect, but doing it carelessly can lock you out if the new configuration rejects your login. Follow a safe verification process: first, keep your current session open. Second, from a separate terminal, attempt a new SSH connection that exercises the changes you plan to enforce — for example, try logging in as a non-root user to confirm keys work. Third, run sudo systemctl restart sshd on the server to reload the configuration. Fourth, immediately test a new connection from the separate terminal. If that test succeeds, you can close the original session. If it fails, review logs via journalctl -u sshd or /var/log/secure to diagnose whether permissions or configuration values are causing rejection. For example, after setting PasswordAuthentication no you must confirm your key login still works. A common operational trap is restarting sshd and then closing the admin connection before verifying a second session works. Use the checklist every time you change sshd_config to maintain access and avoid emergency console recovery. Restarting sshd and safe verification means always test changes from a separate session, restart sshd, and verify a fresh connection before ending your original session.. In practical terms, verify changes without losing access — a safe operational checklist. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Safe restart checklist
keyIdea.text: Always test changes from a separate session, restart sshd, and verify a fresh connection before ending your original session.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Restart & Verify
Checklist
  1. Keep your original admin session open as a rollback path.
  2. From another terminal, attempt a new SSH connection that will validate the change.
  3. Execute sudo systemctl restart sshd to apply changes.
  4. Test the new connection immediately; inspect logs on failure.
Useful commands
sudo systemctl restart sshd
journalctl -u sshd --since "5 minutes ago"
Troubleshoot
If login fails after restart, check permissions for ~/.ssh and authorized_keys, verify the public key is present, and review sshd logs for explicit rejection messages.
Operational tip

Automate backups of sshd_config before edits so you can quickly restore a known-good configuration if required.

screens.title: Client-side SSH configuration (~/.ssh/config)
screens.subtitle: Create host entries for simplified, secure connections

narration.text: The ~/. ssh/config file lets you declare host aliases and connection parameters so you don't type long commands repeatedly. An entry binds a short name to a hostname, user, identity file, and port. For example, create a Host prod-db-01 block with Hostname, User, IdentityFile, and Port configured. After this, connecting requires only ssh prod-db-01. This not only saves time but reduces mistakes like using the wrong key or port. Use clearly named entries and keep identity files in ~/. ssh with strict modes. A subtle behavior is that ssh will try multiple keys by default; specifying IdentityFile prevents unintended attempts which can lead to account lockouts on systems with rate limits. For managing many servers, group entries by environment and add ProxyJump or other directives if you need a bastion host. The recommended practice is to avoid embedding passwords in config and to combine config entries with ssh-agent for passphrase convenience. Always test each host entry after editing the file to confirm it uses the expected key and port. Client-side SSH configuration (~/.ssh/config) means use ~/.ssh/config to map hosts to usernames, keys, and ports so connections are consistent and less error-prone.. In practical terms, create host entries for simplified, secure connections. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Client simplification
keyIdea.text: Use ~/.ssh/config to map hosts to usernames, keys, and ports so connections are consistent and less error-prone.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Client SSH Config
Sample config
# In ~/.ssh/config
Host prod-db-01
    Hostname <IP_ADDRESS_OF_PROD_DB_01>
    User dbadmin
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_rsa_db
    Port 2222
Now run ssh prod-db-01 and ssh will use the specified hostname, user, key, and port automatically.
Best practices
  • Use IdentityFile to avoid ssh trying many keys and hitting rate limits.
  • Keep entries named clearly to avoid confusion across environments.
  • Do not store passphrases or plaintext secrets here; use ssh-agent instead.
Key Takeaway

A correct ~/.ssh/config reduces human error and ensures the intended key and port are used for each host.

screens.title: Managing keys with ssh-agent and ssh-add
screens.subtitle: Hold decrypted private keys in memory for multiple connections without retyping passphrases

narration.text: ssh-agent provides a secure way to keep decrypted private keys in memory for the duration of your session so you do not repeatedly type your passphrase. Start the agent with eval "$(ssh-agent -s)" and add keys using ssh-add path-to-key. Once added, the agent responds to authentication challenges without exposing the private key on disk. This is convenient for multi-server workflows and scripting where repeated connections are needed. Remember to add only what you need and close the agent when finished. On many desktop environments an agent runs automatically and integrates with keyring facilities. A common misconception is that ssh-agent removes the need for a passphrase; it does not — you should still protect keys with strong passphrases. If a workstation is compromised, in-memory keys could be at risk while the agent is running, so use time-limited agent sockets or remove keys using ssh-add -d when not needed. Manage agent lifetime and key addition to balance convenience and security in your environment. Managing keys with ssh-agent and ssh-add means use ssh-agent to hold decrypted keys temporarily and ssh-add to load or remove keys when needed for convenience and security balance.. In practical terms, hold decrypted private keys in memory for multiple connections without retyping passphrases. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Agent management
keyIdea.text: Use ssh-agent to hold decrypted keys temporarily and ssh-add to load or remove keys when needed for convenience and security balance.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › ssh-agent & ssh-add
Common commands
eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_rsa
ssh-add -l   # list keys
ssh-add -d ~/.ssh/id_rsa  # remove key
Add keys once per session to avoid typing your passphrase for every connection. Consider locking your workstation or removing keys when leaving an untrusted environment. On servers, avoid running long-lived agents that keep keys available indefinitely.
Security trade-off
Agent convenience vs. exposure: keys in memory are accessible while the agent runs, so limit lifetime and scope.
Pro tip
Use ssh-add -t to add a key with a timeout if your client supports it, reducing window of exposure.
Key Takeaway

ssh-agent improves usability while keeping the private key encrypted on disk; manage agent lifetime and loaded keys to reduce risk.

screens.title: Revoking and rotating keys
screens.subtitle: Remove compromised keys and rotate keys across systems

narration.text: When a private key is suspected to be compromised, immediate revocation and rotation are required. On each affected server remove the corresponding public key line from ~/. ssh/authorized_keys for that user. Do not simply disable the account unless you want to block administrative access entirely. After removing the public key, restart is not required for authorized_keys changes — they take effect on next login attempt — but review access logs to ensure no unauthorized activity occurred. Next, generate a new key pair on a secure workstation and distribute the new public key to required servers, following the same permission checks. Maintain a record of which key comment or fingerprint maps to which user or device so you can quickly identify and remove entries. A common mistake is forgetting to remove a key from all servers or failing to notify teammates who used the compromised key. Establish a rotation policy and keep backups of safe keys in a secure vault if policy requires recovery. Quick, accurate removal of public keys is the primary remediation step after compromise. Revoking and rotating keys means remove public key lines from authorized_keys and rotate by generating and distributing a new key pair; log and audit the incident.. In practical terms, remove compromised keys and rotate keys across systems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Revocation action
keyIdea.text: Remove public key lines from authorized_keys and rotate by generating and distributing a new key pair; log and audit the incident.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Revoke & Rotate Keys
Immediate steps
  1. Edit ~/.ssh/authorized_keys and remove the compromised public key line.
  2. Check logs (journalctl -u sshd) for suspicious activity tied to that key.
  3. Generate a new key pair on a secure workstation and protect it with a passphrase.
Distribution & audit
Copy the new public key to each server using ssh-copy-id from a secure client, verify permissions, and update any documentation or key inventories with the key fingerprint for future reference.
Mistake to avoid

Do not leave a compromised key listed on some servers. Ensure removal everywhere and rotate keys promptly across your environment.

Key Takeaway

Removal of the public key from authorized_keys is the primary remediation; follow with rotation and audit to restore trusted access.

screens.title: Hands-on activity: implement and test key-based login
screens.subtitle: Guided checklist to perform the lab steps safely on a RHEL server

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks through generating a key pair, copying it to a non-root administrative user, and hardening sshd_config while keeping a recovery path. Step one: run ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "my_admin_key@myclient" and choose a strong passphrase. Step two: start an ssh-agent and add your key. Step three: from your local machine use ssh-copy-id adminuser@<REMOTE_SERVER_IP> to install the public key. Step four: open a separate terminal and verify you can ssh adminuser@<REMOTE_SERVER_IP> without a password. Step five: on the server, edit /etc/ssh/sshd_config and set PasswordAuthentication no, PermitRootLogin no, and AllowUsers adminuser. Step six: restart sshd with sudo systemctl restart sshd and immediately test a new connection from the separate terminal. If all tests pass, close the original session. If a test fails, review permissions for ~/. ssh and authorized_keys and check sshd logs. This step-by-step approach ensures you gain hands-on experience while avoiding lockout risks and building confidence in a repeatable safe workflow. Hands-on activity: implement and test key-based login means generate keys, copy public key, verify from separate session, edit sshd_config, restart sshd, re-test before closing original session.. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Hands-on Activity
Activity: Implement and verify key-based SSH
Client steps
  1. ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "my_admin_key@myclient"
  2. eval "$(ssh-agent -s)" and ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_rsa
  3. ssh-copy-id adminuser@<REMOTE_SERVER_IP>
Server steps
  1. Edit /etc/ssh/sshd_config to set PasswordAuthentication no and PermitRootLogin no
  2. Optionally add AllowUsers adminuser
  3. sudo systemctl restart sshd and test from another session
Remember: keep one session open as a rollback path until you confirm the new settings allow expected access. If a test fails, verify permissions on ~/.ssh and authorized_keys before changing sshd_config back.
Example verification

Open a new terminal and run ssh adminuser@<REMOTE_SERVER_IP> to confirm you can connect with keys before making server hardening permanent.

screens.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.subtitle: Practical traps and the steps that prevent them

narration.text: Administrators commonly make a short list of mistakes when securing SSH. First, editing sshd_config and enabling PasswordAuthentication no without testing key-based access is the number one cause of lockout. Prevent this by keeping an open session and verifying from another terminal. Second, incorrect permissions on ~/. ssh or authorized_keys cause silent key rejection; always set modes right after copying keys. Third, copying the private key by accident onto a server or sharing it via insecure channels compromises credentials; only copy the public key. Fourth, failing to restart sshd after editing sshd_config leads to confusion — remember to restart and check the service status. Fifth, assuming ssh-agent removes the need for a passphrase; an agent improves convenience but you must still protect the private key with a strong passphrase and manage agent lifetime. For each mistake the remedy is a simple operational control: test-first workflows, permission checks, and documented procedures for key distribution and rotation. Treat these as standard operating practices to reduce human error and maintain recoverability. Common mistakes and how to avoid them means test-first changes, correct permissions, never share private keys, restart sshd, and protect keys with passphrases even when using an agent.. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Common Mistakes
Mistake
Disabling passwords before testing
Always verify key login from a separate terminal first.
Mistake
Wrong file permissions
Set ~/.ssh to 700 and authorized_keys to 600 immediately after transfer.
Mistake
Sharing private keys
Never share private keys; only distribute public keys to servers.
Key Takeaway

Adopt test-first processes and permission checks as part of your change routine to avoid the most common SSH hardening failures.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter — part 1

narration.text: Here are the essential concepts to retain. First, SSH is the secure protocol for remote administration; protect it with strong authentication and configuration. Second, key-based authentication uses a private key kept on your workstation and a public key on the server, and a passphrase on the private key provides additional disk protection. Third, ssh-keygen creates key pairs; use a strong algorithm and length and include a helpful comment so you can identify keys later. These ideas form the foundation of SSH security. When you combine strong keys with disciplined file permissions, agent management, and careful server-side directives, you reduce risk and retain operational flexibility. Keep these three items in mind as you practice: protect private keys, verify permissions, and use proper restart and test procedures so changes are effective and reversible.

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Private keys + passphrase + correct permissions make key-based SSH reliable and secure.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter — part 2

narration.text: A few more concise items to retain: ssh-copy-id simplifies installing a public key and sets correct permissions automatically; if not available, use scp and append the public key manually, then set modes. The sshd_config directives PasswordAuthentication no and PermitRootLogin no are central to server hardening and should be coupled with AllowUsers or AllowGroups for narrow access. ssh-agent and ssh-add let you keep decrypted keys available for the session, improving usability without removing passphrase protection. Lastly, always have a recovery plan and use logs to diagnose authentication failures. These practices combined form a practical and repeatable approach to secure SSH access: create strong keys, install them safely, restrict and test server settings, and know how to revoke or rotate keys when needed. Key Concepts means combine tools and safe procedures—ssh-copy-id, sshd directives, ssh-agent, and careful testing—to secure ssh reliably.. ssh-copy-id
Quickly installs your public key and corrects permissions on the server.
sshd_config directives
PasswordAuthentication no, PermitRootLogin no, and AllowUsers restrict authentication methods and accounts.
ssh-agent / ssh-add
Holds decrypted keys in memory to avoid repeated passphrase entry during a session.
Closing summary

Harden SSH by combining key-based auth, permission controls, server directives, and agent management, and always verify changes from a separate session.
